Published October 11, 2017 research-article Copyright © 2017 American Chemical Society Abstract Click to copy section linkSection link copied! Ice is ubiquitous in nature, and heterogeneous ice nucleation is the most common pathway of ice formation. How surface properties affect the propensity to observe ice nucleation on that surface remains an open question. We present results of molecular dynamics studies of heterogeneous ice nucleation on model surfaces. The models surfaces considered emulate the chemistry of kaolinite, an abundant component of mineral dust. We investigate the interplay of surface lattice and hydrogen bonding properties in affecting ice nucleation. We find that lattice matching and hydrogen bonding are necessary but not sufficient conditions for observing ice nucleation at these surfaces. We correlate this behavior to the orientations sampled by the metastable supercooled water in contact with the surfaces. We find that ice is observed in cases where water molecules not only sample orientations favorable for bilayer formation but also do not sample unfavorable orientations. This distribution depends on both surface-water and water–water interactions and can change with subtle modifications to the surface properties. Our results provide insights into the diverse behavior of ice nucleation observed at different surfaces and highlight the complexity in elucidating heterogeneous ice nucleation. Whale, Janine Frohlich-Nowoisky, Mischa Bonn, Angelos Michaelides, and Ellen H.G. Backus,k Department of Chemistry, University of Warwick, Gibbet Hill Road, Coventry CV4 7AL, United Kingdom Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research, Ackermannweg 10, 55128 Mainz, Germany Max Planck Institute for Chemistry, Hahn-Meitner-Weg 1, 55128 Mainz, Germany Yusuf Hamied Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge, Lensfield Road, Cambridge CB2 1EW, United Kingdom kDepartment of Physical Chemistry, University of Vienna, Wahringerstrasse 42, 1090 Wien, Austria E-mail: g.sosso@warwick.ac.uk 1 Abstract The freezing of water into ice is a key process that is still not fully understood. It generally requires an impurity of some description to initiate the heterogeneous nucle- ation of the ice crystals. The molecular structure, as well as the extent of structural order within the impurity in question, both play an essential role in determining its effectiveness. However, disentangling these two contributions is a challenge for both experiments and simulations. In this work, we have systematically investigated the ice-nucleating ability of the very same compound, cholesterol, from the crystalline (and thus ordered) form to disordered self-assembled monolayers. Leveraging a combina- tion of experiments and simulations, we identify a "sweet spot" in terms of the surface coverage of the monolayers, whereby cholesterol maximises its ability to nucleate ice (which remains inferior to that of crystalline cholesterol) by enhancing the structural order of the interfacial water molecules. These findings have practical implications for the rational design of synthetic ice-nucleating agents. 2 Introduction The formation of ice from supercooled liquid water is one of the most important phase transitions: it plays a role in global phenomena such as climate change 1-3 and it is key to transformative medical treatments such as regenerative and reproductive medicine, 4-7 as the storing of biological material relies on cryopreservation protocols where it is essential to control the extent of ice formation in cells. In nature, ice almost always forms thanks to the help of impurities which lower the free energy cost of creating an ice nucleus large enough to grow into an actual ice crystal. 1,8 This process is known as heterogeneous nucleation, and it exploits specific impurities, which range from mineral dust 1,9-11 to bacterial fragments. 12-16 However, what exactly makes such substances effective in facilitating the nucleation of ice remains to be fully understood. In recent years, both experiments and simulations have made substantial progress in the field. 8,10,17-29 For instance, recent evidence suggests that the activity of a given ice- nucleating agent (INA) might be due to an interplay between the order within said agent (e.g., its crystalline, ordered nature, or the presence of specific defects) and its molecular structure, particularly the presence of specific functional groups (the hydroxyl -OH group is a common example). 30-34 However, which characteristic - the degree of order or the presence of functional groups - is most important, is unknown, as disentangling the two different contributions is a challenge for both experiments and simulations. 8,34 In fact, more often than not, we seek to gain insight into ice nucleation by comparing the effectiveness of different materials, thus acting on both order and molecular structure at the same time. Here, we answer this crucial question by adopting a different approach, namely probing the ice-nucleating ability of the same substance, cholesterol (CHL), in different forms, from its crystalline phase 35 to self-assembled monolayers, 36,37 characterised by a variable degree of order and flexibility. Cholesterol is an interesting model system to study since it is an effective ice-nucleating agent and a number of steroids with molecular structure similar to CHL show equally strong ice-nucleating ability in their crystalline phases. 38,39 In this work, 3 we have isolated the impact of structural order only, by systematically investigating the ice-nucleating ability of the very same compound, cholesterol, from the crystalline (and thus ordered) form to disordered self-assembled monolayers, thus focusing in detail on the impact of structural order on heterogeneous ice nucleation without having to compare the ice-nucleating efficiency of different materials. By bringing together state-of-the-art experimental techniques and atomistic computer simulations, we find that CHL monolayers display a weaker ice-nucleating activity compared to CHL crystals. A systematic investigation of CHL monolayers characterised by different coverages (and thus different degrees of structural order as well as flexibility) reveals that the degree of order of the CHL molecules within the monolayers has a direct impact on the population of pre-critical ice nuclei forming at the CHL-water interfaces. In particular, there exists a specific interval of CHL coverages that maximises the ability of this steroid to order interfacial water molecules in such a way as to facilitate ice nucleation. This systematic investigation of the impact of order and disorder on the ice-nucleating ability of a biologically relevant compound allows us to unravel the microscopic motivations underpinning its activity and offer valuable practical guidelines toward the rational design of the next generation of INAs. In particular, our results imply that more emphasis should be placed on the supra-molecular aspects of biological INAs as opposed to their molecular structure. fetched_contents.title: ACP - Parameterizing ice nucleation rates using contact angle and activation energy derived from laboratory data
fetched_contents.text: ACP 15 Dec 2008 | 15 Dec 2008 Parameterizing ice nucleation rates using contact angle and activation energy derived from laboratory data Abstract. The rate of ice nucleation in clouds is not easily determined and large discrepancies exist between model predictions and actual ice crystal concentration measured in clouds. In an effort to improve the parameterization of ice nucleating in cloud models, we investigate the rate of heterogeneous ice nucleation under specific ambient conditions by knowing the sizes as well as two thermodynamic parameters of the ice nuclei – contact angle and activation energy. Laboratory data of freezing and deposition nucleation modes were analyzed to derive inversely the two thermodynamic parameters for a variety of ice nuclei, including mineral dusts, bacteria, pollens, and soot particles. The analysis considered the Zeldovich factor for the adjustment of ice germ formation, as well as the solute and curvature effects on surface tension; the latter effects have strong influence on the contact angle. Contact angle turns out to be a more important factor than the activation energy in discriminating the nucleation capabilities of various ice nuclei species. By extracting these thermodynamic parameters, laboratory results can be converted into a formulation that follows classical nucleation theory, which then has the flexibility of incorporating factors such as the solute effect and curvature effect that were not considered in the experiments. Due to various uncertainties, contact angle and activation energy derived in this study should be regarded as "apparent" thermodynamics parameters.

fetched_contents.text: Classical nucleation theory Theory of nucleation Classical nucleation theory (CNT) is the most common theoretical model used to quantitatively study the kinetics of nucleation.[1][2][3][4] Nucleation is the first step in the spontaneous formation of a new thermodynamic phase or a new structure, starting from a state of metastability. The kinetics of formation of the new phase is frequently dominated by nucleation, such that the time to nucleate determines how long it will take for the new phase to appear. The time to nucleate can vary by orders of magnitude, from negligible to exceedingly large, far beyond reach of experimental timescales. One of the key achievements of classical nucleation theory is to explain and quantify this immense variation.[5] Description The central result of classical nucleation theory is a prediction for the rate of nucleation R {\displaystyle R} , in units of (number of events)/(volume·time). For instance, a rate R = 1000 m − 3 s − 1 {\displaystyle R=1000\ {\text{m}}^{-3}{\text{s}}^{-1}} in a supersaturated vapor would correspond to an average of 1000 droplets nucleating in a volume of 1 cubic meter in 1 second. The CNT prediction for R {\displaystyle R} is[3] R = N S Z j exp ⁡ ( − Δ G ∗ k B T ) {\displaystyle R\ =\ N_{S}Zj\exp \left(-{\frac {\Delta G^{*}}{k_{B}T}}\right)} where * Δ G ∗ {\displaystyle \Delta G^{*}} is the free energy cost of the nucleus at the top of the nucleation barrier, and k B T {\displaystyle k_{B}T} is the average thermal energy with T {\displaystyle T} the absolute temperature and k B {\displaystyle k_{B}} the Boltzmann constant. * N S {\displaystyle N_{S}} is the number of nucleation sites. * j {\displaystyle j} is the rate at which molecules attach to the nucleus. * Z {\displaystyle Z} is the Zeldovich factor, (named after Yakov Zeldovich[6]) which gives the probability that a nucleus at the top of the barrier will go on to form the new phase, rather than dissolve. This expression for the rate can be thought of as a product of two factors: the first, N S exp ⁡ ( − Δ G ∗ / k B T ) {\displaystyle N_{S}\exp \left(-\Delta G^{*}/k_{B}T\right)} , is the number of nucleation sites multiplied by the probability that a nucleus of critical size has grown around it. It can be interpreted as the average, instantaneous number of nuclei at the top of the nucleation barrier. Free energies and probabilities are closely related by definition.[7] The probability of a nucleus forming at a site is proportional to exp ⁡ [ − Δ G ∗ / k T ] {\displaystyle \exp[-\Delta G^{*}/kT]} . So if Δ G ∗ {\displaystyle \Delta G^{*}} is large and positive the probability of forming a nucleus is very low and nucleation will be slow. Then the average number will be much less than one, i.e., it is likely that at any given time none of the sites has a nucleus. The second factor in the expression for the rate is the dynamic part, Z j {\displaystyle Zj} . Here, j {\displaystyle j} expresses the rate of incoming matter and Z {\displaystyle Z} is the probability that a nucleus of critical size (at the maximum of the energy barrier) will continue to grow and not dissolve. The Zeldovich factor is derived by assuming that the nuclei near the top of the barrier are effectively diffusing along the radial axis. By statistical fluctuations, a nucleus at the top of the barrier can grow diffusively into a larger nucleus that will grow into a new phase, or it can lose molecules and shrink back to nothing. The probability that a given nucleus goes forward is Z {\displaystyle Z} . Taking into consideration kinetic theory and assuming that there is the same transition probability in each direction, it is known that x 2 = 2 D t {\displaystyle x^{2}=2Dt} . As Z j {\displaystyle Zj} determines the hopping rate, the previous formula can be rewritten in terms of the mean free path and the mean free time λ 2 = 2 D τ {\displaystyle \lambda ^{2}=2D\tau } . Consequently, a relation of Z j {\displaystyle Zj} in terms of the diffusion coefficient is obtained > Z j = 1 τ = 2 D λ 2 {\displaystyle Zj={\frac {1}{\tau }}={\frac {2D}{\lambda ^{2}}}} . Further considerations can be made in order to study temperature dependence. Therefore, Einstein-Stokes relation is introduced under the consideration of a spherical shape > D = k B T 6 π η λ {\displaystyle D={\frac {k_{B}T}{6\pi \eta \lambda }}} , where η {\displaystyle \eta } is the material's viscosity. Considering the last two expressions, it is seen that Z j {\displaystyle Zj} ∝ T {\displaystyle \propto T} . If T ≈ T m {\displaystyle T\approx T_{m}} , being T m {\displaystyle T_{m}} the melting temperature, the ensemble gains high velocity and makes Z j {\displaystyle Zj} and Δ G ∗ {\displaystyle \Delta G^{*}} to increase and hence, R {\displaystyle R} decreases. If T ≪ T m {\displaystyle T\ll T_{m}} , the ensemble has a low mobility, which makes R {\displaystyle R} to decrease as well. To see how this works in practice we can look at an example. Sanz and coworkers[8] have used computer simulation to estimate all the quantities in the above equation, for the nucleation of ice in liquid water. They did this for a simple but approximate model of water called TIP4P/2005. At a supercooling of 19.5 °C, i.e., 19.5 °C below the freezing point of water in their model, they estimate a free energy barrier to nucleation of ice of Δ G ∗ = 275 k B T {\displaystyle \Delta G^{*}=275k_{B}T} . They also estimate a rate of addition of water molecules to an ice nucleus near the top of the barrier of j = 10 11 s − 1 {\displaystyle j=10^{11}\ {\text{s}}^{-1}} and a Zeldovich factor Z = 10 − 3 {\displaystyle Z=10^{-3}} . The number of water molecules in 1 m3 of water is approximately 1028. ## How surface properties determine ice nucleation efficiency

The evidence indicates that ice nucleation efficiency is strongly influenced by a combination of surface chemistry, orientation, and local water structure, rather than a single property. The strongest correlate in the provided sources is **surface-water orientation and hydrogen bonding compatibility**, because the Langmuir study states that ice nucleation is observed when water molecules sample orientations favorable for bilayer formation and do not sample unfavorable orientations [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that surface lattice and hydrogen bonding are necessary but not sufficient conditions [N1-F1]. This means that **hydrogen bonding and molecular orientation** are among the most important surface properties correlated with ice nucleation efficiency.

### Water adsorption, hydrogen bonding, and hydrophobicity
Water adsorption and hydrogen bonding are closely linked in the evidence. The Langmuir study explicitly frames the problem as the interplay of surface properties and water orientations, and it notes that the water–water interactions and the surface-water interactions determine the orientation distribution of metastable water [N1-F1]. The same study concludes that hydrogen bonding is important because it helps water adopt favorable orientations for ice nucleation [N1-F1]. A separate source on water’s properties explains that water’s orientation-dependent hydrogen bonding leads to open tetrahedral cage-like structuring, which is relevant to ice-related behavior [N1-R2]. This implies that **surface hydrogen-bonding capability and the ability to stabilize favorable water orientations** are central to nucleation efficiency.

Hydrophobicity is also relevant but more indirect. The hydrophobic effects source says that nonpolar molecules tend to aggregate in water, and the hydrophobic ice source says that bilayer ice is favored by maximizing hydrogen bonds [N1-R5][N1-R3]. Together, these suggest that hydrophobic surfaces can influence nucleation by altering the balance between water adsorption and hydrogen bonding, but the evidence does not directly state that hydrophobicity alone is the strongest predictor. The most defensible conclusion from the provided material is that **hydrophobicity and related surface hydrophilicity can affect nucleation by changing the thermodynamics of water adsorption and hydrogen-bonding accessibility** [N1-R5][N1-R3][N1-R2].

### Surface curvature and roughness
Surface curvature and roughness are important because they create favorable nucleation sites. The structural-order study on ice nucleation says that rough surfaces can disrupt crystalline ordering and may make nucleation unfavorable, but it also notes that molecularly rough surfaces with the same hydrophobicity can behave differently [N2-R5]. The Cambridgeshire study on structural order further states that the degree of order of the CHL molecules within the monolayer has a direct impact on pre-critical ice nuclei formation [N2-F2]. Taken together, these sources indicate that **local curvature and roughness can create a heterogeneous surface landscape** that either enhances or suppresses nucleation, depending on whether the surface supports favorable orientation sampling and order.

The rough-surface study is especially relevant here because it shows that **roughness alone is not sufficient to determine nucleation efficiency; the effect depends on the interplay between geometry and surface chemistry** [N2-R5]. This means roughness can act as a **site-generating feature** rather than a universal enhancer of efficiency.

### Surface charge or functional groups
Surface charge and functional groups modify nucleation propensity through their influence on hydrogen bonding, orientation, and interfacial water structure. The Langmuir study discusses the interplay of surface lattice and hydrogen bonding [N1-F1], and the cholesterol study emphasizes that the degree of order of the monolayer molecules affects interfacial water structure and ice nucleation [N2-F2]. While the provided evidence does not list explicit charge measurements, it does support the broader principle that **surface chemistry and functional-group presence affect the energetics of water adsorption and hydrogen bonding**, which in turn affect nucleation propensity [N1-F1][N2-F2].

A separate source on hydroxyl groups on graphene surfaces shows that increasing hydroxyl density increases ice nucleation activity [N3-R4]. This is strong evidence that **functional groups can directly alter nucleation efficiency by introducing specific hydrogen-bonding or orientation-preferencing sites** [N3-R4]. The evidence therefore supports a conclusion that **surface chemistry and functional groups are important determinants of nucleation efficiency** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R4].

### Summary
The most strongly correlated surface properties are **surface-water orientation compatibility, hydrogen bonding capability, and local chemical functionality** [N1-F1][N1-R2][N3-R4]. Water adsorption and hydrogen bonding are central because they determine whether metastable water can adopt favorable orientations for ice nucleation [N1-F1][N1-R2]. Hydrophobicity is relevant but more indirect, as it affects adsorption and hydrogen-bonding accessibility rather than being a standalone predictor [N1-R5][N1-R3]. Curvature and roughness create favorable nucleation sites, but their effect depends on surface chemistry and orientation compatibility [N2-R5][N2-F2]. Surface charge and functional groups modify nucleation propensity mainly through their influence on hydrogen bonding and interfacial structure [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R4].

## How structural features determine ice nucleation efficiency

The evidence suggests that ice nucleation efficiency is heavily shaped by **structural order, defects, phase transitions, and interfacial mobility**. The strongest direct support comes from the structural-order study, which says that the ice-nucleating ability of cholesterol can be enhanced when the surface coverage creates a “sweet spot” of interfacial water ordering, even though the monolayer itself is less active than crystalline cholesterol [N2-F2]. This implies that **structural order and disorder in the surface layer can shift nucleation barriers and nucleation site availability**.

### Crystal defects, grain boundaries, and phase transitions
The provided evidence does not give a direct experimental catalog of defects or grain boundaries, but it does support the general principle that **structural heterogeneity can create a distribution of nucleation sites**. The structural-order study notes that the same compound is studied in crystalline and disordered self-assembled monolayers, and the difference in order affects ice nucleation ability [N2-F2]. The rough-surface study also suggests that surface geometry can disrupt crystalline ordering and thereby influence nucleation [N2-R1]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that **defects, phase transitions, and structural disorder can act as heterogeneous nucleation sites or barriers, depending on whether they favor or hinder the formation of an ice nucleus** [N2-R1][N2-F2].

### Molecular ordering and interfacial mobility
Molecular ordering is central to the evidence. The structural-order study explicitly states that the degree of order of the CHL molecules within the monolayer has a direct impact on the population of pre-critical ice nuclei at the CHL-water interface [N2-F2]. It also identifies a coverage interval that maximizes the ability of cholesterol to order interfacial water molecules, which in turn facilitates ice nucleation [N2-F2]. The same source implies that **interfacial mobility** matters because the ordered monolayer can support a more favorable water structure for nucleation [N2-F2]. The Langmuir study similarly emphasizes that surface lattice and hydrogen bonding affect ice nucleation through the orientations sampled by metastable water [N1-F1].

The theoretical framework in the nucleation theory sources reinforces this picture. Classical nucleation theory states that the nucleation barrier is much lower for heterogeneous nucleation than for homogeneous nucleation, and that the barrier depends on the surface area and the thermodynamics of the system [N4-R2][N4-F4]. The structural-order evidence shows that **molecular ordering can lower the effective nucleation barrier by stabilizing favorable interfacial water structures** [N2-F2]. This suggests that **interfacial mobility and the ability to form ordered water layers are key factors in reducing nucleation barriers** [N2-F2][N4-F4].

### Structural heterogeneity and distribution of nucleation sites
Structural heterogeneity is especially important because it can create a **distribution of nucleation sites** rather than a uniform response. The structural-order study shows that the same compound behaves differently depending on its degree of order, which means that different structural states support different nucleation efficiencies [N2-F2]. The rough-surface study notes that molecularly rough surfaces with the same hydrophobicity can behave differently, indicating that **local structural heterogeneity can alter the nucleation landscape** [N2-R5]. The Langmuir study also supports this by showing that the orientation distribution of water depends on both surface-water and water–water interactions, and that this distribution changes with subtle surface modifications [N1-F1].

The evidence therefore supports a broad conclusion: **structural heterogeneity creates a population of sites with different nucleation propensities**, which can explain why some surfaces are more active than others even if they are chemically similar [N2-F2][N2-R5][N1-F1]. This is especially relevant for natural surfaces such as mineral dust, where defects, grain boundaries, and phase transitions can all contribute to the observed ice-nucleating activity.

### Summary
Structural features that most strongly determine ice nucleation efficiency are **surface order, defects, grain boundaries, and phase transitions**, with the evidence especially strong for **molecular ordering and interfacial mobility** [N2-F2][N2-R1][N4-R2][N4-F4]. Ordered interfacial layers can stabilize favorable water orientations and reduce nucleation barriers, while structural disorder can create a heterogeneous nucleation landscape [N2-F2][N1-F1]. Structural heterogeneity is important because it often produces a distribution of nucleation sites rather than a single uniform response [N2-F2][N2-R5]. In short, the structural environment determines nucleation efficiency by controlling the energetic and geometric conditions under which ice nuclei can form [N2-F2][N4-F4].

## How to compare and quantify nucleator efficiency across different materials

The evidence indicates that comparing and quantifying nucleator efficiency requires careful attention to both **mechanistic metrics** and **experimental artifacts**, because ice nucleation efficiency depends on surface properties, structure, and environmental conditions. The most useful metrics in the provided sources are **contact angle, activation energy, nucleation rate, and thermodynamic parameterization**, while the evidence also cautions that **intrinsic nucleation ability must be distinguished from experimental artifacts**.

### Which experimental metrics capture nucleator efficiency reliably?
The most reliable metrics are those that connect nucleation ability to thermodynamic and kinetic parameters. The ACP paper states that heterogeneous ice nucleation can be parameterized using **contact angle and activation energy**, and that laboratory data can be converted into a formulation consistent with classical nucleation theory [N3-F3]. It also says that contact angle is a more important factor than activation energy in distinguishing nucleation capabilities among different ice nuclei species [N3-F3]. This suggests that **contact angle and activation energy are useful quantitative indicators**, but they should be treated as apparent parameters because of experimental uncertainties [N3-F3].

The nucleation-rate study supports a complementary view: ice nucleation efficiency can be inferred from the rate of heterogeneous nucleation, and the rate depends on the number of nucleation sites, the Zeldovich factor, and the exponential dependence on the nucleation barrier [N4-F4]. The evidence therefore supports a quantitative approach in which **nucleation rate, contact angle, and activation energy** are used together to compare materials [N3-F3][N4-F4].

### How to interpret contact angle, AFM, and nucleation rate measurements
Contact angle is useful because it reflects the thermodynamic compatibility between the surface and water. The ACP paper explicitly ties contact angle to the nucleation capability of different ice nuclei species [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that contact angle is influenced by solute and curvature effects, and that it is more important than activation energy for discrimination [N3-F3]. This means that contact angle should be interpreted as a **surface-water compatibility indicator**, not a direct measure of ice nucleation efficiency alone [N3-F3].

AFM is also relevant as a characterization tool. The microplastics study uses **XPS and 3D AFM** with ice nucleation experiments to characterize surfaces [N3-R2]. The laponite study uses AFM to characterize particle morphology and lateral size distribution [N3-R3]. These examples show that AFM provides **morphological and surface-characterization evidence**, which is important for interpreting nucleation behavior. However, AFM itself is not a nucleation rate metric; it is best used in combination with nucleation experiments to understand why a surface is active [N3-R2][N3-R3].

Nucleation rate measurements are directly quantitative, but the evidence also emphasizes that they depend on thermodynamic and kinetic factors. The ACP paper says that nucleation rates can be converted into a formulation consistent with classical nucleation theory using contact angle and activation energy [N3-F3]. The nucleation theory source explains that heterogeneous nucleation rates depend on the number of nucleation sites, the Zeldovich factor, and the exponential dependence on the free-energy barrier [N4-F4]. So, **nucleation rate should be interpreted as a kinetic proxy**, while **contact angle and activation energy provide thermodynamic context** [N3-F3][N4-F4].

### How to distinguish intrinsic nucleation ability from experimental artifacts
The evidence strongly supports the need to separate intrinsic nucleation ability from experimental artifacts. The cholesterol study notes that the same compound can behave differently depending on its degree of order, and that the observed nucleation ability is not simply a fixed property of the material itself [N2-F2]. The microplastics study also shows that weathering can enhance ice-nucleating activity, implying that **preparation and exposure conditions can alter observed efficiency** [N6-R2]. The ACP paper explicitly warns that contact angle and activation energy should be regarded as “apparent” thermodynamic parameters because of various uncertainties [N3-F3].

The AFM/XPS study further illustrates artifact susceptibility by using both surface characterization and ice nucleation experiments to avoid misattributing activity to surface morphology alone [N3-R2]. The temperature-dependent anti-icing study also highlights that contact angle and ice–substrate contact area can be affected by ice nucleation itself rather than surface wettability [N6-R5]. This means that **artifact susceptibility is especially high when measurements are taken near freezing temperatures or when ice nucleation is not fully controlled** [N6-R5].

### Summary
To compare and quantify nucleator efficiency reliably, the most useful metrics are **contact angle, activation energy, and nucleation rate**, with the evidence favoring contact angle as the more informative thermodynamic parameter [N3-F3][N4-F4]. AFM and other characterization methods help interpret the surface structure and morphology that underlie nucleation behavior [N3-R2][N3-R3]. However, intrinsic nucleation ability must be distinguished from experimental artifacts, because preparation, exposure, and measurement conditions can strongly influence the observed activity [N2-F2][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The evidence therefore supports a cautious quantitative approach: use thermodynamic metrics to rank materials, combine them with kinetic nucleation measurements, and characterize the surface structure with AFM or XPS to explain differences [N3-F3][N4-F4][N3-R2][N3-R3].

## How nucleator efficiency depends on environmental conditions and measurement setup

The evidence indicates that ice nucleation efficiency is highly sensitive to **temperature, humidity, pressure, nucleation mode, and sample preparation/exposure**. The provided sources show that these factors can alter the observed efficiency by changing the thermodynamics of water adsorption, the availability of favorable orientations, and the measurement conditions.

### How temperature, humidity, and pressure influence observed nucleation efficiency
Temperature is central because it affects both the free-energy barrier and the Zeldovich factor in nucleation theory. The nucleation theory source states that the nucleation rate depends on the exponential of the free-energy barrier over thermal energy, and that the Zeldovich factor itself depends on temperature [N4-F4]. It also notes that at very low temperatures, mobility decreases, making nucleation slower [N4-F4]. The anti-icing study adds that contact angle and ice–substrate contact area were mainly affected by ice nucleation rather than surface wettability at −30 °C [N6-R5]. This implies that **near-freezing temperatures can amplify the effects of nucleation on observed surface behavior**.

Humidity is also important because it controls water availability and adsorption. The AFM/XPS study notes that contact angle measurements were conducted under 50–60% relative humidity [N6-R4]. The weathering study shows that weathering can enhance ice-nucleating activity, which suggests that **environmental exposure can change the surface hydrophobicity, functional groups, and adsorbed water layer**, thereby altering nucleation efficiency [N6-R2]. The evidence therefore supports the view that **humidity and temperature are not neutral; they can change the effective nucleation environment** [N4-F4][N6-R4][N6-R5].

Pressure is less explicitly discussed, but the theoretical framework implies that pressure affects the thermodynamic state of the system. Since classical nucleation theory is based on free-energy barriers and kinetic factors, any pressure change that alters the density or phase behavior of water or the nucleating material would influence the observed efficiency [N4-F4]. However, the provided evidence does not give a direct pressure-dependent comparison, so this conclusion is more inferential than direct.

### How nucleation mode changes comparisons
The evidence indicates that the choice of nucleation mode matters for comparisons. The ACP paper explicitly states that it analyzed laboratory data of freezing and deposition nucleation modes [N3-F3]. This is important because different modes can emphasize different aspects of nucleation: freezing mode may favor certain sites, while deposition mode may measure different kinetic pathways [N3-F3]. The cholesterol study also shows that the same compound can behave differently under different structural conditions, which implies that **mode-specific effects can change how nucleation efficiency is expressed** [N2-F2].

The anti-icing study further shows that the interpretation of contact angle and ice–substrate contact area depends on whether ice nucleation is the dominant factor [N6-R5]. This implies that **nucleation mode can affect not only the observed efficiency, but also the way surface properties are measured** [N6-R5]. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that **direct comparisons between materials should be made under the same nucleation mode and controlled conditions** [N3-F3][N6-R5].

### How sample preparation and exposure affect artifact susceptibility
Sample preparation and exposure are major sources of artifact susceptibility. The microplastics study shows that weathering can enhance ice-nucleating activity, meaning that **preparation history matters** [N6-R2]. The anti-icing study notes that contact angle and ice–substrate contact area can be influenced by ice nucleation itself, not just by surface wettability [N6-R5]. This indicates that **preparation and exposure can alter the surface chemistry, morphology, and adsorbed layer, making the observed efficiency less intrinsic** [N6-R2][N6-R5].

The AFM/XPS study also highlights artifact susceptibility by combining characterization with nucleation experiments [N3-R2]. ## Integrated explanation of how surface and structural features affect ice nucleation efficiency

Ice nucleation efficiency is determined by a combination of **surface properties**, **structural features**, **environmental conditions**, and **measurement setup**. The branch reports together show that the most important factors are not isolated chemical or physical properties, but rather the interplay between water orientation, hydrogen bonding, surface chemistry, molecular ordering, defects, and the thermodynamics of nucleation. Below I synthesize those findings into a coherent explanation.

---

## 1) Surface properties are central to ice nucleation efficiency

The surface property branch report emphasizes that ice nucleation efficiency depends strongly on **surface chemistry, orientation compatibility, and local water structure** [N7]. The most directly correlated surface properties are:

- **Surface-water orientation compatibility**: Ice nucleation is observed when water molecules sample orientations favorable for bilayer formation and do not sample unfavorable orientations [N1-F1].
- **Hydrogen bonding capability**: The Langmuir study explicitly frames the problem as the interplay of surface properties and water orientations, and it notes that both surface-water and water–water interactions determine the orientation distribution of metastable water [N1-F1]. A separate source on water’s properties explains that orientation-dependent hydrogen bonding leads to open tetrahedral cage-like structuring, which is relevant to ice-related behavior [N1-R2].
- **Hydrophobicity and hydrophilicity**: These affect nucleation by changing the thermodynamics of water adsorption and hydrogen-bonding accessibility, but the evidence does not treat hydrophobicity as a standalone predictor [N1-R5][N1-R3][N1-R2].
- **Surface curvature and roughness**: Roughness can create favorable nucleation sites, but its effect depends on whether the surface supports favorable orientation sampling and order [N2-R5][N2-F2].
- **Surface charge and functional groups**: These modify nucleation propensity through their influence on hydrogen bonding and interfacial structure [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R4].

### Key synthesis
The strongest evidence is that **surface properties are most strongly correlated with ice nucleation efficiency when they control water adsorption, hydrogen bonding, and orientation compatibility** [N1-F1][N1-R2][N3-R4]. Hydrophobicity and roughness are important, but their effect is indirect and context-dependent [N1-R5][N2-R5]. Surface chemistry and functional groups matter because they shape the interfacial water structure that facilitates or suppresses nucleation [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R4].

---

## 2) Structural features shape nucleation efficiency through order, defects, and interfacial mobility

The structural features branch report shows that ice nucleation efficiency is heavily shaped by **structural order, defects, phase transitions, and interfacial mobility** [N8]. The evidence is especially strong on the role of **molecular ordering and interfacial mobility**.

- **Crystal defects, grain boundaries, and phase transitions**: The evidence does not provide a direct catalog of defects, but it supports the general principle that **structural heterogeneity can create a distribution of nucleation sites**. The same compound studied in crystalline and disordered self-assembled monolayers shows that the degree of order strongly affects nucleation ability [N2-F2]. The rough-surface study also notes that surface geometry can disrupt crystalline ordering and may make nucleation unfavorable, while molecularly rough surfaces with the same hydrophobicity can behave differently [N2-R1][N2-R5].
- **Molecular ordering and interfacial mobility**: Ordered interfacial layers can stabilize favorable water orientations and reduce nucleation barriers, while structural disorder can create a heterogeneous nucleation landscape [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The structural-order study explicitly states that the degree of order of the surface layer has a direct impact on the population of pre-critical ice nuclei [N2-F2].
- **Interfacial mobility**: The evidence implies that mobility matters because ordered monolayers can support favorable interfacial water structure, while disordered layers may not [N2-F2].

### Key synthesis
Structural features most strongly determine ice nucleation efficiency when they control **molecular ordering and interfacial mobility** [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-F4]. Ordered interfacial layers can stabilize favorable water orientations and lower nucleation barriers, while defects, grain boundaries, and phase transitions can create a heterogeneous nucleation landscape [N2-F2][N2-R1][N2-R5]. In other words, the structural environment determines whether ice nuclei can form by controlling both the energetic conditions and the geometric distribution of sites [N2-F2][N4-F4].

---

## 3) How to compare and quantify nucleator efficiency across materials

The comparison branch report argues that reliable comparison requires combining **thermodynamic and kinetic metrics**, because nucleator efficiency depends on both the intrinsic nucleation ability and the measurement setup [N9].

- **Contact angle and activation energy**: The ACP paper states that heterogeneous ice nucleation can be parameterized using contact angle and activation energy, and that contact angle is more important than activation energy in distinguishing nucleation capabilities among different ice nuclei species [N3-F3]. It also warns that these parameters should be regarded as “apparent” thermodynamic parameters because of experimental uncertainties [N3-F3].
- **Nucleation rate**: The nucleation theory source explains that heterogeneous nucleation rates depend on the number of nucleation sites, the Zeldovich factor, and the exponential dependence on the free-energy barrier [N4-F4]. This means nucleation rate should be interpreted as a kinetic proxy rather than a direct measure of intrinsic activity [N4-F4].
- **AFM and other characterization methods**: AFM provides morphological and surface-characterization evidence, which is important for interpreting nucleation behavior [N3-R2][N3-R3]. However, AFM alone is not sufficient to quantify nucleation efficiency; it must be combined with nucleation experiments.
- **Distinguishing intrinsic ability from experimental artifacts**: The evidence strongly supports caution. The cholesterol study shows that the same compound can behave differently depending on its degree of order [N2-F2]. The weathering study shows that weathering can enhance ice-nucleating activity, implying that preparation and exposure conditions can alter observed efficiency [N6-R2]. The anti-icing study notes that contact angle and ice–substrate contact area can be affected by ice nucleation itself rather than surface wettability [N6-R5].

### Key synthesis
The most reliable metrics for comparing nucleator efficiency are **contact angle, activation energy, and nucleation rate**, with contact angle being the more informative thermodynamic parameter [N3-F3][N4-F4]. AFM and XPS help interpret the surface structure and morphology underlying nucleation behavior [N3-R2][N3-R3]. However, intrinsic nucleation ability must be distinguished from experimental artifacts because preparation, exposure, and measurement conditions can strongly influence the observed activity [N2-F2][N6-R2][N6-R5].

---

## 4) Environmental conditions and measurement setup strongly affect observed efficiency

The environmental branch report shows that ice nucleation efficiency is highly sensitive to **temperature, humidity, pressure, nucleation mode, and sample preparation/exposure** [N10].

- **Temperature**: Temperature affects both the free-energy barrier and the Zeldovich factor in nucleation theory. At very low temperatures, mobility decreases, making nucleation slower [N4-F4]. The anti-icing study also notes that contact angle and ice–substrate contact area were mainly affected by ice nucleation rather than surface wettability at −30 °C [N6-R5].
- **Humidity**: Humidity influences water availability and adsorption. The evidence also notes that contact angle measurements were conducted under controlled relative humidity [N6-R4]. Weathering can alter surface hydrophobicity, functional groups, and adsorbed water layer, thereby changing nucleation efficiency [N6-R2].
- **Pressure**: The evidence does not provide a direct pressure-dependent comparison, but the theoretical framework implies that pressure can affect the thermodynamic state of the system [N4-F4].
- **Nucleation mode**: Different modes can emphasize different nucleation pathways. The ACP paper explicitly analyzed freezing and deposition nucleation modes [N3-F3]. The anti-icing study further shows that nucleation mode can affect how surface properties are interpreted [N6-R5].
- **Sample preparation and exposure**: Weathering and preparation history matter because they can change the surface chemistry, morphology, and adsorbed layer [N6-R2][N6-R5]. The AFM/XPS study illustrates artifact susceptibility by combining characterization with nucleation experiments [N3-R2].

### Key synthesis
Observed nucleation efficiency depends strongly on **temperature, humidity, and nucleation mode**, with the evidence strongest on temperature and humidity [N4-F4][N6-R4][N6-R5]. Pressure is relevant inferentially, as it alters the thermodynamic state of the system [N4-F4]. Nucleation mode changes comparisons because different modes emphasize different pathways [N3-F3]. Sample preparation and exposure are especially important because they can change surface chemistry, morphology, and adsorbed layer, making the observed activity artifact-prone [N6-R2][N6-R5][N3-R2].

---

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the four branches support a unified conclusion: **ice nucleation efficiency is determined by the combined action of surface chemistry, molecular ordering, defects, interfacial mobility, and environmental conditions**. The most important mechanisms are:

1. **Water adsorption and hydrogen bonding**: These determine whether metastable water can adopt favorable orientations for ice nucleation [N1-F1][N1-R2].
2. **Surface curvature and roughness**: These create favorable nucleation sites, but only if they support compatible orientation sampling and order [N2-R5][N2-F2].
3. **Molecular ordering and interfacial mobility**: Ordered interfacial layers can stabilize favorable water structures and lower nucleation barriers, while disorder can create a heterogeneous nucleation landscape [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-F4].
4. **Structural defects and phase transitions**: These can act as heterogeneous nucleation sites or barriers, depending on whether they favor or hinder ice nucleus formation [N2-R1][N2-R5].
5. **Environmental conditions**: Temperature, humidity, and nucleation mode strongly influence observed efficiency [N4-F4][N6-R4][N6-R5].
6. **Measurement and artifact control**: Contact angle, activation energy, and nucleation rate are useful metrics, but they must be interpreted carefully and combined with AFM/XPS-type surface characterization to distinguish intrinsic ability from artifacts [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R2].

### Practical implication
If you want to understand why one solid nucleator is more efficient than another, the best approach is to ask: **how does its surface support favorable water orientations and hydrogen bonding?** and **what structural disorder or order does it have at the interface?** The answer will also depend on whether the nucleation was measured under immersion, contact freezing, or deposition conditions, and whether temperature and humidity were controlled [N3-F3][N4-F4][N6-R5].

In short, surface and structural features affect ice nucleation efficiency by shaping the thermodynamic and kinetic environment in which ice nuclei can form, while environmental and measurement conditions determine how that efficiency is observed [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4][N6-R5].

Taken together, the four branches support a unified conclusion: **ice nucleation efficiency is determined by the combined action of surface chemistry, molecular ordering, defects, interfacial mobility, and environmental conditions**. The most important mechanisms are:

1. **Water adsorption and hydrogen bonding**: These determine whether metastable water can adopt favorable orientations for ice nucleation [N1-F1][N1-R2].
2. **Surface curvature and roughness**: These create favorable nucleation sites, but only if they support compatible orientation sampling and order [N2-R5][N2-F2].
3. **Molecular ordering and interfacial mobility**: Ordered interfacial layers can stabilize favorable water structures and lower nucleation barriers, while disorder can create a heterogeneous nucleation landscape [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-F4].
4. **Structural defects and phase transitions**: These can act as heterogeneous nucleation sites or barriers, depending on whether they favor or hinder ice nucleus formation [N2-R1][N2-R5].
5. **Environmental conditions**: Temperature, humidity, and nucleation mode strongly influence observed efficiency [N4-F4][N6-R4][N6-R5].
6. **Measurement and artifact control**: Contact angle, activation energy, and nucleation rate are useful metrics, but they must be interpreted carefully and combined with AFM/XPS-type surface characterization to distinguish intrinsic ability from artifacts [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R2].

### Practical implication
If you want to understand why one solid nucleator is more efficient than another, the best approach is to ask: **how does its surface support favorable water orientations and hydrogen bonding?** and **what structural disorder or order does it have at the interface?** The answer will also depend on whether the nucleation was measured under immersion, contact freezing, or deposition conditions, and whether temperature and humidity were controlled [N3-F3][N4-F4][N6-R5].

In short, surface and structural features affect ice nucleation efficiency by shaping the thermodynamic and kinetic environment in which ice nuclei can form, while environmental and measurement conditions determine how that efficiency is observed [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4][N6-R5].
